nameStory: The bur oak gets its name from its distinctive acorns, which are surrounded by a deeply fringed cap that looks like a mossy, bristly bur. This 'bur' is actually the cupule - the cap that holds the acorn - and it can cover up to three-quarters of the massive acorn. Some folks also call it the mossycup oak for this very reason!
description: Bur oak is a mighty tree that can grow into one of the largest oaks in North America, reaching 80 feet tall with a broad, spreading crown. Its most famous feature is producing the biggest acorns of any North American oak - some as large as golf balls! The tree has distinctive deeply-lobed leaves with rounded edges and thick, rugged bark that becomes deeply furrowed with age. This is a member of the white oak group, known for their sweet acorns that wildlife absolutely love.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The acorns are absolutely huge - the largest of any North American oak - often 1-2 inches long and sitting in a distinctive fringed cap that covers much of the nut. The cap looks mossy or bur-like with thread-like scales that feel soft and bristly to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large leaves (6-12 inches) with deep, rounded lobes that create a distinctive fiddle or cross shape. The lobes are much deeper than most oaks, often extending nearly to the midrib, and feel thick and leathery with smooth, rounded edges.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark is deeply furrowed with thick, scaly ridges that feel rough and corky. On younger trees, the bark is lighter gray and smoother, gradually developing the characteristic deep furrows as the tree ages.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Develops a massive, broad crown with thick, sturdy branches that often spread wider than the tree is tall. Young trees may look scrubby, but mature specimens become true giants with impressive, spreading canopies.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Winter buds are small, rounded, and reddish-brown, clustered at the tips of thick, stout twigs. The buds feel smooth and are less pointed than red oak group members.

habitat: In New England, bur oak is quite rare and typically found in rich, well-drained soils of river valleys and bottomlands. It prefers open areas or woodland edges and is more commonly found in western New England where conditions are slightly drier. This tree is really more at home in the Midwest prairies, so finding one in New England is always a special discovery.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late April to early May, unfolding from small reddish buds. Tiny yellowish-green flowers appear with the leaves - males in drooping catkins, females as small spikes.
seasonality.summer: Full leafed out with distinctive deeply-lobed foliage providing dense shade. Young acorns begin developing and are visible by mid-summer as small green nuts in their characteristic fringed caps.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to brown, sometimes with orange tints, before dropping. The massive acorns ripen and fall, making this the best time to spot the diagnostic huge nuts with their mossy caps.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's impressive architecture with thick, spreading limbs. Look for the distinctive deeply-furrowed bark and small clustered buds at twig tips.

funFact: A single mature bur oak can produce up to 700 pounds of acorns in a good year, and these sweet nuts were so important to Native Americans that they would actually manage prairies with controlled burns to help bur oaks thrive - the thick, corky bark helps these trees survive fires that would kill other species!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with white oak, but bur oak's leaves are much more deeply cut (almost to the midrib) and the acorns are dramatically larger with that distinctive fringed, mossy cap. Memory trick: 'Bur' sounds like 'big' - both the leaves' lobes and the acorns are bigger than other oaks!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'scrub oak' in some regions, don't let that fool you - this is actually one of the most massive oak species and can live over 400 years. The 'scrub' name comes from how it looks when young or when growing in harsh prairie conditions where it stays smaller.
compareHints: Among New England oaks, bur oak is easily distinguished by its enormous acorns with fringed caps and extremely deeply-lobed leaves. White oak has similar rounded leaf lobes but they're much shallower, and its acorns are much smaller with smooth caps. The other white oak group members like swamp white oak and chestnut oak have completely different leaf shapes - more oval with teeth rather than deep lobes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England oaks, white oak is distinguished by its evenly rounded leaf lobes without bristle tips (unlike red oak group species) and its light gray bark.

Among New England's oaks, northern red oak is distinguished by its pointed leaf lobes (white oak has rounded lobes), its large size (much bigger than bear oak or dwarf chinkapin oak), and its relatively shallow acorn caps (deeper than scarlet oak, shallower than pin oak).
Bear oak stands apart from other New England oaks by being consistently shrubby rather than tree-like, even at maturity.
Among the red oak group, black oak has the deepest leaf lobes - much deeper than red oak or pin oak.
Unlike white oak with its deeply rounded lobes, chestnut oak has scalloped edges with rounded teeth.
Among New England's white oak group, swamp white oak is unique in its preference for wet areas and its distinctive leaf shape with deeper bottom lobes.
Among New England's red oaks, scarlet oak stands out with its deeply dissected leaves that have the most pronounced sinuses (indentations).
Unlike other New England oaks that have lobed leaves (deeply indented edges), dwarf chinkapin oak has simple leaves with rounded teeth like a saw blade.
English oak stands out among New England's oaks by having the leaf and acorn stems completely reversed from most natives - very short leaf stems but very long acorn stems.
Among New England oaks, pin oak stands out for its combination of deeply-cut leaves with sharp points and its distinctive pin-like branching pattern.
Among New England oaks, post oak is unique for its cross-shaped leaves with rounded lobes and fuzzy undersides.
Unlike most New England oaks, chinkapin oak has toothed rather than lobed leaves, setting it apart immediately from white oak, red oak, and others.
Unlike our native oaks, Turkey oak has those telltale bristly buds and bristle-tipped leaves that you can actually feel.
Sawtooth oak is completely different from all other New England oaks because of its simple, toothed leaves rather than the lobed leaves found on species like white oak, red oak, or black oak.
Among New England oaks, willow oak is unmistakable due to its unlobed, willow-like leaves - all other regional oaks have distinctly lobed or toothed leaves.
Among New England oaks, shingle oak is instantly recognizable by its simple, unlobed leaves - all other common oaks in the region have the typical lobed leaves we associate with oaks.
